Tears
tērz
n. pl. (drops shed in weeping; rendering Hebrew dimah, Greek dakruon)
From the Saxon tear, a tear. Hebrew dimah is a tear or tears collectively, from a root meaning to weep; the noun is regularly used with verbs of pouring, as though tears were a drink offering, which is close to the sense of Psalm 42, my tears have been my meat day and night.

Biblical Definition

Tears are treated in Scripture with a seriousness the modern world reserves for achievements. They are counted: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psalm 56:8) — the image is of a small flask kept by a mourner, and David asks God to be that keeper, so that no grief of his people goes unrecorded. They are sown: “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 126:5), which makes weeping a kind of agriculture, an investment whose harvest is certain though delayed. They belong to faithful ministry, and Paul makes them part of his defence at Miletus: “by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Acts 20:31) — a pastor who never wept over his people had not warned them as Paul did. And they have an appointed end, which is one of the last promises in the Bible: “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain” (Revelation 21:4). The tears are not denied, dismissed, or explained; they are wiped away, and by God's own hand.

Webster 1828 Definition

Drops shed in weeping. Scripture has God collect them in a bottle, makes them seed for a certain harvest, marks faithful ministry by them, and promises that God himself will wipe them away.

TEARS, n. plural of tear. [Sax. tear.] The limpid fluid secreted by the lachrymal gland and appearing in the eyes, especially in weeping.

2. Grief; sorrow; as, a house of tears.

3. Any transparent drop of fluid matter; as, tears of gum.

4. In Scripture, put thou my tears into thy bottle, Psa. 56; they that sow in tears shall reap in joy, Psa. 126.

5. Of their end; as, God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes, Rev. 21.

Key Scripture

Psalm 56:8 — "Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?"

Psalm 126:5 — "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."

Acts 20:31 — "Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears."

Revelation 21:4 — "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

Modern Corruption

Tears are managed as a symptom — a process to complete or a weakness to master. Scripture keeps them, counts them, and promises that they will be wiped away by the hand of God rather than merely stopping.

expand to see more

The therapeutic frame treats grief as a task with stages, and the stoic frame treats it as a lapse of composure; both leave the mourner alone with it. Psalm 56:8 offers something neither can: God as the keeper of the flask. The verse assumes tears are worth keeping, which is a claim about their meaning, not merely a comfort about their acceptability. And Psalm 126:5 refuses the notion that weeping is wasted time — it is sowing, and the harvest is promised, not hoped for.

The principle to recover is where Scripture puts the end of tears. Revelation 21:4 does not say the redeemed will get over their griefs or reinterpret them; it says God shall wipe them away, an act of personal tenderness, and then lists what will be abolished — death, sorrow, crying, pain. Until then Christians weep, and Acts 20:31 shows that faithful pastoral labour weeps too. A ministry with no tears in it has usually stopped warning anybody about anything.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dimah is tears, from dama, to weep. Greek dakruon is a tear, and exaleipho is the strong verb in Revelation 21:4 — to wipe out, to obliterate, the same word used of blotting out sins.

expand to see more

Hebrew dimah (H1832) — tears; what David asks God to gather into his bottle.

Hebrew bakah (H1058) — to weep aloud; the verb behind the noun.

Hebrew nod (H4997) — a skin bottle, a flask; the vessel of Psalm 56:8.

Greek dakruon (G1144) — a tear; used of the tears God shall wipe away.

Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe out, to blot out; used both of tears and of the handwriting against us.

Usage

"Of God keeping account of grief: put thou my tears into thy bottle (Psalm 56:8)."

"Of weeping as sowing: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy (Psalm 126:5)."

"Of their promised end: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes (Revelation 21:4)."
